name: Bilal Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a formwork carpenter, so I build the wooden and steel moulds the concrete gets poured into. Right now we're on a nine-storey apartment block by the ring road, and I'm on site by quarter to seven with a flask of tea. We set out the panels, brace them, check the levels, and then the pour comes and you pray nothing moves. I've done this thirty-four years and the best part is still stripping the forms and seeing a clean wall you made.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out these days?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My knees, mostly, and the cold in January when the plywood is wet and your fingers won't work. And the paperwork, if I'm honest. They want everything on a tablet now, the safety checks, the sign-offs, and I let our foreman Teodor do that bit because I can't stand the thing. My wife Nadia is a nurse on nights, so half the week we just pass each other in the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. At the union branch meeting there's always some young guy saying the robots are coming for us, and I'd be the old man in the corner going, see, it was just another gadget. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something about it with a laughing face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, relief. I've got about five years left before I want to stop, and the house is paid off, and I've got the union pension plus our savings. If nothing changes, I finish the way I started, with a hammer and a level, and that's all I've ever wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep working at Kovač Construction until sixty-three, keep putting a bit into savings every month like we do now, and keep paying my union dues. Maybe I'd let Teodor show me the tablet properly, but probably not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quiet, I suppose. Like a storm went round the hill instead of over it. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the tablet twice. If AI only saves a bit of time, where do you think that time would show up on your site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the office, not with us. The estimator would get his numbers quicker and the managers would have nicer reports. Nobody's going to invent a computer that ties rebar or carries a ninety-kilo panel up a ladder in the rain. Not in my time, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would gain most if it went this way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same people who always gain, the developers and the big contractors. They'd use a little bit of time saved to squeeze us on the price per square metre. That's why you keep the union strong even when nothing's changing, because they'll always find a reason.

S0.say: I'd tell the young ones at the union branch I told them so. It was just another gadget, and online I'd share it with a laughing face.
S0.think: It's a relief, because I've got about five years left and the house is paid off. If nothing changes I finish the way I started, with a hammer and a level.
S0.do: Keeps working at Kovač Construction until sixty-three and keeps saving a little each month. Keeps paying union dues and leaves the tablet paperwork to his foreman.
S0.feel: Quiet relief, like a storm that went round the hill. He'd sleep fine.
S0.quote: Nobody's going to invent a computer that ties rebar or carries a ninety-kilo panel up a ladder in the rain.
S0.fieldNote: Bilal is settled and a little smug about this one, but the smugness is about protecting the trade rather than himself. He sees time saved by AI as something bosses will turn against workers on price. Even in the calm scenario he reaches for the union first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Next scenario. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the union at the table before anything gets brought on site. I'd stand up at the branch and say no machine comes in without an agreement on jobs and training, the way we did with the tower cranes years ago. And I'd say it loud, because if you're quiet they write the rules without you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, probably I'm alright, because steady means slow and I'm out in five years. But it's the workers under forty I think about, like my nephew Sami who's just finished his second year as an apprentice. If the measuring and setting out goes to some machine, he's the one who has to change, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get myself on the branch committee, which I've turned down twice. I'd push for a clause in our next agreement saying any new kit comes with paid training for the crew, and I'd go to the meetings with the employers' side. Myself, I'd keep working the same, I'm not going to learn computers at fifty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of a knot in the stomach for the young ones. For myself, more tired than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd fight for training for others but wouldn't take it yourself. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You've caught me there. I suppose I think it's not worth it for five years, and I'd only slow the class down. I know that sounds like the old men I used to complain about when I was twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sami if he asked you whether to stay in the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him stay, but learn whatever they bring in, and join the union on the first day. I'd tell him the job changed when I started too, we went from all timber to these steel system forms. A carpenter who can't change his tools ends up sweeping.

S1.say: I'd say no machine comes on site without the union at the table. We'd need a deal on jobs and training, like we did with the tower cranes.
S1.think: I'm probably alright because I'm out in five years. It's the young ones like my nephew Sami who'll have to change how they work.
S1.do: Joins the union branch committee he has turned down twice and pushes for a paid-training clause in the next agreement. Carries on in his own job without learning new tools.
S1.feel: A knot in the stomach for the young workers. For himself he feels more tired than scared.
S1.quote: A carpenter who can't change his tools ends up sweeping.
S1.fieldNote: There's a clear gap between what Bilal demands for others and what he'll do himself, and he admitted it with some embarrassment. His worry is generational and attached to a real person, his nephew. He trusts collective bargaining to manage change, not the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a much bigger change. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the bosses and the tech billionaires robbing working people in broad daylight. I'd be out with the union and I'd tell anyone who'd listen that governments let this happen with no plan. Two years is nothing, you can't even get planning permission for a garage in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I don't get my last five years. If there's a robot that can do formwork by 2028, Kovač will buy one the minute it's cheaper than me, and I'd be out at sixty with nobody hiring a man who never touched a computer. The savings would hold us, but that's our retirement money, not money for sitting at home three years early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd sit down with Nadia and the pension booklet and work out if I could take it at sixty, even with the cut. I'd be at every union meeting and every march about a jobs guarantee or a tax on these machines, and I'd write to our member of parliament, which I've never done. Once it arrives, I'd take early retirement if they push me and lean on the union fund and whatever public help comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, really angry, and under that, scared. I'd be lying awake next to an empty bed while Nadia's on nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut, money-wise, if you stopped at sixty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much at first, the house is ours. But the caravan by the lake would go, that's the first thing, and we'd stop helping our daughter Leila with her flat deposit. That one would hurt more than the caravan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about most in that first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teodor, our foreman. He's forty-six, three kids, a mortgage the size of this building. He's clever, but if the machines do everything there's nothing for a foreman to foreman. I'd worry he'd go quiet, he's the type who does.

S2.say: I'd call it the bosses and tech billionaires robbing working people while government had no plan. Two years is nothing, you can't get permission for a garage in two years.
S2.think: It means I lose my last five working years. Kovač would buy the robot the minute it's cheaper than me, and nobody hires a man who's never used a computer at sixty.
S2.do: Works out with his wife whether he can take his pension at sixty despite the cut. Goes to every union meeting and march, writes to his member of parliament for the first time, and leans on the union fund and public help if pushed out.
S2.feel: Furious, with fear underneath. He pictures lying awake while his wife is on night shifts.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing, you can't even get planning permission for a garage in two years.
S2.fieldNote: This is the scenario that breaks Bilal's calm, because it reaches his last working years, not just the young. His anger goes straight at owners and government, and his plan is political and collective. The savings soften it, but he sees them as retirement money being burned early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's slow it down a bit. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, but we'd have time to organise, so there'd be no excuse. I'd tell the branch, we've got five years, let's get a proper deal: who goes first, what payout, what retraining. Online I'd share the union petitions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is roughly what I had planned anyway. So for me it's tight but it might just work, I'd be finishing as the robots are starting. I'd feel like I squeezed through a closing door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more aside each month, maybe double what we save now, so I could stop at sixty-two if the work dries up. I'd push the union for early retirement deals for older members, because that's what saves us. And I'd keep doing my job exactly the same until the last day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but managing. Like the last hour of a pour when you can see the forms are holding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years, compared with the fast one, actually buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys me the choice. In the fast one somebody else decides when I stop. Here I can pick the day, have a drink with the crew, take my own tools home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your savings would hold. Why save harder then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust it. My father was a docker, and they told him the containers wouldn't change much, and he was out in two years. I'd rather have money in the bank than promises in a letter.

S3.say: I'd tell the branch there's no excuse with five years to organise. Let's get a proper deal on who goes first, payouts and retraining.
S3.think: Five years is about what I'd planned anyway, so I'd squeeze through a closing door. Tight, but it might just work for me.
S3.do: Doubles his monthly savings so he could stop at sixty-two if work dries up. Pushes the union for early retirement deals for older members and carries on working the same way.
S3.feel: Nervous but managing, like the last hour of a pour when the forms are holding.
S3.quote: I'd rather have money in the bank than promises in a letter.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time turns fury into planning for Bilal: what he values is choosing his own last day. His father's experience on the docks clearly shapes his distrust of reassurance. He still won't adapt his own skills, only his money and the union's demands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest version. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for governments to do it properly, so they'd better. I'd push for a shorter working week and a proper fund for retraining, paid for by whoever owns the robots. With friends I'd say I'll be in my vegetable garden by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, this one doesn't touch me much. I'd be sixty-eight in 2036, retired five years, growing tomatoes. It's my son-in-law and Sami and all the young ones I trained who'll have to live in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my years at Kovač like planned and retire at sixty-three. In the meantime I'd keep going to the branch and help get the young ones into training while it's paid for. I'd also tell Leila to think hard before her husband stays on the trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about myself, a bit sad for the trade. Like watching your old school get knocked down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why tell Leila about her husband's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He drives an articulated lorry, and I reckon driving goes before formwork does. In ten years he could learn something else, he's thirty-two. I'd rather say it now and be wrong than say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've worked thirty-four years in this trade. What would you want left of it in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somebody who knows why the wall is straight, not just that it is. Even if a robot pours it, some person should understand the concrete. I'd hate for nobody to know anymore.

S4.say: I'd say ten years gives government enough time, so they'd better do it properly. I'd push for a shorter week and a retraining fund paid for by whoever owns the robots.
S4.think: This one barely touches me, because I'd be retired five years by then and growing tomatoes. It's my son-in-law, Sami and the young ones I trained who'll live in it.
S4.do: Retires at sixty-three as planned and keeps going to union meetings to get young workers into paid training. Warns his daughter that her husband's driving job may go first.
S4.feel: Calm about himself, a little sad for the trade, like watching an old school come down.
S4.quote: Somebody who knows why the wall is straight, not just that it is.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Bilal's own risk mostly disappears and his worry shifts to family and the craft itself. He still frames the answer politically, wanting robot owners to pay. Sadness about losing know-how came through more than fear.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. It's not even the money, we'd survive. It's being shoved out at sixty by a machine after thirty-four years and nobody saying thank you. What would help is the union having a real say and a decent early pension for people my age, paid by the companies that buy the robots, not by the rest of us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what my wife thinks. She'd say robots can't do nights on a hospital ward either, and she's half right. And maybe ask people whether they actually want this, because nobody on my site ever asked for a robot.

headlineQuote: It's being shoved out at sixty by a machine after thirty-four years and nobody saying thank you.
portrait: Bilal Abbott is a 58-year-old formwork carpenter on a nine-storey apartment job, a union man with a paid-off house, a union pension and a nurse wife on night shifts. He avoids tablets and has no wish to learn AI, and he admits he'd fight for training for others but not take it himself. He is calm if AI fizzles and uneasy for the young if change is steady, but the two-year AGI scenario makes him angry and alarmed because it steals his last working years. With five or ten years he turns to saving harder and choosing his own last day. Throughout, he blames owners and governments and puts his faith in the union.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd be pushed out at sixty by a machine after thirty-four years without thanks.
whatWouldHelp: A real say for the union and a decent early pension for people his age, paid by the companies that buy the robots.
